formation.title: The Mandate Restored
formation.text:
The fractured lands of China are united once more beneath a single sovereign. The Mandate of Heaven, that ancient compact between ruler and cosmos, has passed to a dynasty that has proven its worthiness through conquest and governance alike. The Middle Kingdom stands restored. But the question of how to wield this immense power remains.

The bureaucratic traditions of millennia offer one path: perfect the imperial administration, extend the examination system, draw all authority to the Dragon Throne. The tributary states will acknowledge celestial supremacy, and the realm will be governed by scholars trained in the classics.

But the seas call with a different promise. The shipyards of the coast can launch fleets that dwarf anything the world has seen. The maritime silk road carries porcelain, silk, and tea to every shore. China's wealth need not stop at its borders. It can flow outward on the tide.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: The Dragon Throne commands All Under Heaven

modifiers.name: Celestial Authority
modifiers.text: The Son of Heaven rules All Under Heaven. The Mandate restored, the Imperial bureaucracy reaches into every province, every prefecture, every village. The examination halls fill with scholars, the censors root out corruption, and the authority of the Dragon Throne radiates outward like the sun itself. All peoples within the realm bend toward the center.

options.text: Let the treasure fleets carry our civilization to every shore

modifiers.name: Maritime Ascendancy
modifiers.text: The treasure fleets of the Middle Kingdom sail forth once more, their sails darkening the horizon from the South China Sea to the coasts of Africa. The shipyards of Nanjing and Longjiang thunder with construction, the merchants of Canton and Quanzhou grow fat on the profits of the maritime silk road, and the Dragon Banner flies over harbors that have never seen its like.

advances.name: Junk Tradition
advances.text: China's maritime heritage stretches back millennia. The ocean-going junk (with its watertight compartments, balanced rudder, and battened sails) is the most advanced vessel of its age. From the Song dynasty's naval victories to the coastal trade routes, Chinese shipbuilding represents an unbroken tradition of maritime engineering.

advances.name: Keju Examination System
advances.text: The imperial examination system selects officials through rigorous testing of classical learning, literary composition, and policy analysis. This meritocratic institution, refined over centuries, produces a governing class of scholar-bureaucrats whose loyalty runs to the throne rather than to regional lords.

advances.name: Silk Weaving Tradition
advances.text: Chinese silk production, perfected over four millennia, remains unmatched anywhere in the world. The state-sponsored weaving workshops of Suzhou, Hangzhou, and Nanjing produce fabrics of extraordinary quality that command premium prices on every trade route from the steppe to the Mediterranean.

advances.name: Treasure Fleet
advances.text: The grand shipyards of Longjiang and Nanjing launch the largest vessels the world has ever seen. The treasure fleet, hundreds of ships carrying thousands of sailors and soldiers, projects Chinese power across the Indian Ocean, from Southeast Asia to the coast of Africa.

advances.name: Naval Levy System
advances.text: The coastal populations of Fujian, Zhejiang, and Guangdong provide experienced sailors and shipwrights for the imperial navy. These maritime communities, with their generations of seafaring tradition, form the backbone of China's naval power.

advances.name: Imperial Kilns
advances.text: The imperial porcelain factory at Jingdezhen, established under the Hongwu Emperor, transforms the city into the porcelain capital of the world. Directly administered by the court, the kilns produce wares of unparalleled quality: a single imperial order can demand hundreds of thousands of pieces.

advances.name: Yongle Grandeur
advances.text: The Yongle Emperor's ambitious construction program (the Forbidden City, the restoration of the Grand Canal, the expansion of Beijing) represents the most concentrated burst of imperial construction since the Qin dynasty. These projects reshape the physical landscape of China itself.

advances.name: Divine Machine Battalion
advances.text: The Shenjiying, one of the three elite divisions of the capital garrison, is devoted entirely to firearms operations. Armed with hand cannons, multiple rocket launchers, and proto-muskets described in the Huolongjing, these troops represent the cutting edge of gunpowder warfare.

event.title: The Divine Machine Battalion
event.text:
The Shenjiying, the Divine Machine Battalion, represents a revolution in military organization. Founded to harness the devastating potential of gunpowder weapons that China itself invented, this elite formation combines arquebusiers, rocketers, and cannoneers into a disciplined fighting force unlike anything the world has seen.

The fire lance, the world's first gunpowder weapon, was a Chinese invention. Now its descendants (the hand cannon, the matchlock, the volley gun) are organized into permanent military divisions with standardized equipment and regular drill. The Huolongjing, the Fire Dragon Manual, codifies these weapons and their tactical employment. The question is whether to commit fully to this firearms revolution or to maintain it as one tool among many.

options.text: The Shenjiying shall be the vanguard of our armies

modifiers.name: Legacy of the Shenjiying
modifiers.text: The Divine Machine Battalion's innovations in gunpowder warfare continue to influence Chinese military doctrine.

options.text: A worthy addition to our military tradition

advances.name: Firearm Levies
advances.text: The success of the Shenjiying model inspires the extension of firearms training to the broader levy system. Provincial garrisons increasingly equip their troops with gunpowder weapons, creating a nationwide reserve of trained firearms operators.

advances.name: Haijin Coastal Defense
advances.text: The Haijin maritime prohibition policy, whatever its effects on trade, drives the construction of an extensive coastal defense network. Fortified watchtowers, naval patrol stations, and garrison posts line the coast from Liaodong to Guangdong, forming a defensive chain against wokou pirates and foreign intruders.

advances.name: Grand Canal Mastery
advances.text: The restored Grand Canal, stretching over 1,700 kilometers from Hangzhou to Beijing, is the longest artificial waterway in the world. Millions of laborers maintain its locks, embankments, and feeder channels. This engineering marvel binds north and south China together, carrying grain, silk, and porcelain to the capital and knitting the empire's economy into a single fabric.

advances.name: Single Whip Reform
advances.text: Zhang Juzheng's sweeping tax reform consolidates the bewildering array of Ming-era taxes (land tax, labor service, local levies, tribute obligations) into a single payment in silver. Comprehensive land surveys, the redrawn fish-scale registers, and direct silver collection nearly triple state revenues within a decade.

event.title: The Single Whip Reform
event.text:
The grand minister Zhang Juzheng has proposed a sweeping transformation of the imperial tax system. The current maze of land taxes, labor obligations, and tribute payments (levied in grain, silk, silver, and corvee labor across dozens of separate categories) would be consolidated into a single silver payment. The fish-scale registers will be redrawn, the land resurveyed, and the gentry's tax evasion confronted directly.

The numbers speak for themselves: silver revenues could nearly triple within a decade. But this reform strikes at the privileges of the landed gentry, the very class that staffs the bureaucracy. And tying all taxation to silver makes the empire dependent on the flow of foreign silver through maritime trade: a vulnerability that could prove dangerous if that flow is ever disrupted.

options.text: Implement the Single Whip across all provinces

modifiers.name: Single Whip Efficiency
modifiers.text: The consolidation of taxes into a single silver payment has streamlined revenue collection across the empire.

options.text: The reform is sound in principle

advances.name: Fuchuan Warship
advances.text: The fuchuan, the 'blessed ship', is the backbone of the Chinese ocean-going navy. These large, flat-bottomed vessels carry heavy armament, accommodate large crews, and can navigate both coastal shallows and open ocean. Armed with bronze cannons and fire arrows, the fuchuan represents Chinese naval power in the age of sail.

advances.name: Porcelain Trade Dominance
advances.text: Chinese porcelain, 'white gold' to the Europeans who covet it, dominates global luxury trade. The kilns of Jingdezhen produce millions of pieces annually, exported through Canton and the maritime silk road to markets in Japan, Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. No competitor can match the quality, scale, or variety of Chinese ceramic production.

advances.name: Mandarin Duck Formation
advances.text: General Qi Jiguang's innovative twelve-man 'mandarin duck' formation combines pikemen, swordsmen, shieldmen, and wolf-brush wielders into a flexible tactical unit designed to counter the fast-moving wokou raiders. This combined-arms approach, codified in Qi's military treatises, represents a new standard of tactical sophistication.

advances.name: Canton System
advances.text:
The Qing government's restriction of all foreign maritime trade to the single port of Canton creates a controlled commercial environment where the Thirteen Factories, licensed Chinese merchant houses, serve as intermediaries between Western traders and the Chinese interior. The system generates enormous customs revenue while keeping foreign influence contained.

Available in: Imperial Porcelain Kiln

advances.name: Banner Integration
advances.text: The expansion of the Eight Banners system to incorporate Mongol and Han Chinese units creates a multiethnic imperial military. The twenty-four banners (eight Manchu, eight Mongol, eight Han) provide a permanent garrison force stationed in strategic cities across the empire, integrating diverse warrior traditions into a unified command structure.

advances.name: Encyclopedic Compilations
advances.text: The massive literary projects of the Qing court (the Kangxi Dictionary, the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, the Collected Statutes) represent the most ambitious program of knowledge compilation in human history. The Siku Quanshu alone encompasses over 36,000 volumes, preserving and systematizing the entirety of Chinese intellectual heritage.

advances.name: Self-Strengthening Movement
advances.text: The Yangwu Movement, 'foreign affairs movement', represents China's first systematic attempt at military and industrial modernization. The Jiangnan Arsenal in Shanghai, the Fuzhou Shipyard, the Tianjin Military Academy, and dozens of smaller facilities bring Western industrial technology to Chinese soil under the principle of 'Chinese essence, Western methods.'

event.title: The Self-Strengthening Movement
event.text:
The humiliations of recent decades have made one thing painfully clear: the Middle Kingdom's military technology has fallen behind the Western barbarians. A coalition of reform-minded officials (Li Hongzhang, Zeng Guofan, Zuo Zongtang) advocate a program of selective modernization. 'Chinese learning for the essential principles, Western learning for practical application,' they argue.

The Jiangnan Arsenal in Shanghai, the Fuzhou Shipyard, the Tianjin Military Academy: these institutions represent a new China, one that masters foreign technology without abandoning its own civilization. But conservatives at court question whether Western methods can be adopted without Western ideas following close behind. Can the empire modernize its arms while preserving the Confucian order?

options.text: Adopt Western methods: the empire must be strong

modifiers.name: Self-Strengthening Momentum
modifiers.text: The arsenals and academies of the Self-Strengthening Movement drive rapid modernization of Chinese industry and military.

options.text: Preserve the essential principles of our civilization

modifiers.name: Yangwu Traditionalism
modifiers.text: The preservation of Confucian principles alongside selective modernization sustains the cultural authority of the Middle Kingdom.

advances.name: Tongzhi Restoration
advances.text: The Tongzhi Restoration represents a concerted effort to revitalize the Qing dynasty through a return to Confucian governance principles combined with practical administrative reform. The suppression of the Taiping and Nian rebellions, the reorganization of provincial administration, and the reinvigoration of the examination system demonstrate that the old order retains both vitality and legitimacy.

advances.name: Maritime Customs Modernization
advances.text: The establishment of the Imperial Maritime Customs Service under foreign-supervised but Chinese-owned management introduces modern accounting, standardized tariffs, and efficient revenue collection to China's port system. The customs revenue becomes a reliable source of income for the central government and a model for administrative modernization.

advances.name: Reform Spirit
advances.text: The spirit of reform that animated the Hundred Days of 1898, however briefly, represents a vision of comprehensive institutional modernization: a modern educational system, a constitutional government, an industrial economy. Though the initial movement was crushed, its ideas cannot be unthought. The genie of reform, once released, reshapes every subsequent political debate.

destiny.name: The Mandate Endures
destiny.text: China is reunified and the Mandate of Heaven secured. The Middle Kingdom now stands at a crossroads: will it turn inward to perfect its celestial administration, or outward to project its civilization across the seas? Stability is paramount: the realm must be at peace before the great work can begin.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: The Mandate Endures
event.text:
The Middle Kingdom is whole once more. The fractured warring states have been brought to heel, the mandate secured through conquest and wisdom alike. The Dragon Throne stands supreme over the most populous and productive civilization on earth.

But supremacy demands direction. The empire's resources are vast but not infinite. The question that has haunted every dynasty since the First Emperor now confronts us: in which direction shall the Middle Kingdom grow?

options.text: The mandate is secure: for now

destiny.name: Pacify the Frontiers
destiny.text: The kingdoms of the south have long challenged imperial authority. Bring Dali in the mountains of Yunnan under the Dragon Banner and extend the mandate into Dai Viet. Only when the frontiers are secure can the empire turn its attention to greater ambitions.

conditions.text: Chose Celestial Authority
Own Tàihé, or a subject owns it
Own Thăng Long, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 1000

event.title: The Frontiers Pacified
event.text:
The kingdom of Dali in the mountains of Yunnan has been brought under imperial authority, and Dai Viet acknowledges the Dragon Throne. For the first time in centuries, the empire's frontiers are truly secure.

The generals who achieved these victories now look to the court for their next orders. The bureaucracy is already extending its reach into the newly pacified territories, establishing examination halls and tax registers where once there was only chaos.

options.text: The frontier generals have earned their rewards

destiny.name: The Nine Provinces United
destiny.text: The ancient ideal of the Nine Provinces encompassed all civilized lands under heaven. Bring Kashgar and Samarkand into the imperial sphere to demonstrate that no corner of the Western Regions lies beyond the Dragon Throne's reach. The southern capital on the Yangtze is built up until its wealth matches the empire's territorial ambitions.

conditions.text: Own Kashgar, or a subject owns it
Own Samarkand, or a subject owns it
Shangyuan (Nanjing) is ours and has been built up to a development of at least 62
Army size at least 50

event.title: The Nine Provinces United
event.text:
The ancient dream of the Nine Provinces, all civilized lands under one sovereign, approaches reality. The oasis cities of the Tarim and Samarkand's bazaars now operate under the protection of the Dragon Banner. The empire stretches from the Yangtze to the banks of the Oxus.

This achievement demands a choice in governance. Some ministers advocate strengthening the mandate through diplomatic prestige and loyal subjects, using the empire's growing spy networks to prevent rebellion before it starts. Others argue for a program of military fortification: garrison the frontiers with permanent forces, invest in siege capabilities, and make the empire literally impregnable.

options.text: Rule through the mandate's moral authority

modifiers.name: Mandate's Vigor
modifiers.text: The moral authority of the Dragon Throne commands loyalty from subjects and respect from foreign courts. Imperial agents monitor every province for signs of disloyalty.

options.text: Fortify every border and garrison every pass

modifiers.name: Frontier Garrisons
modifiers.text: Permanent military garrisons along every frontier make the empire impregnable. Siege engineers stand ready to reduce any fortress that dares resist imperial authority.

destiny.name: All Under Heaven
destiny.text: Tianxia, All Under Heaven, is not merely a phrase but a destiny. When the Dragon Throne commands from Delhi to the Ili, when the capital at Dadu has grown to twice its size and no rival can match the empire's military strength, the Mandate of Heaven becomes universal fact. Build the Forbidden Palace as the seat of this eternal administration.

conditions.text: Own Delhi, or a subject owns it
Own Almaliq, or a subject owns it
Dadu is ours and has been built up to a development of at least 90
Prestige at least 75
Army size at least 75

event.title: All Under Heaven
event.text:
Tianxia is achieved. The Dragon Throne commands an empire of unprecedented scope: from the subcontinental plains to the Central Asian steppes, from the tropical south to the frozen north. No dynasty in Chinese history has ruled so much, so firmly.

The scholars at court debate the meaning of this achievement. The hawks argue that universal empire demands universal preparedness: the army traditions, the diplomatic machinery, the mechanisms of war must be perfected to maintain this dominion forever. The Confucian idealists counter that true universal rule requires harmony, and the empire should heal its conquered lands, build its prestige through cultural achievement, and let the sheer weight of its civilization make rebellion unthinkable.

modifiers.name: Universal Empire
modifiers.text: The mechanisms of universal dominion are perfected: a professional military tradition, efficient diplomatic machinery, and the authority to dictate terms to any adversary.

options.text: Let celestial harmony govern All Under Heaven

modifiers.name: Celestial Harmony
modifiers.text: The empire governs through harmony rather than force. Devastated lands recover quickly under benevolent administration, and the dynasty's prestige endures across generations.

destiny.name: Reopen the Sea Routes
destiny.text: The Haijin restrictions choked China's natural maritime advantage. Reverse this isolation: seize the chokepoint at Malacca and ensure silk flows through markets under imperial influence. The sea routes that once carried Zheng He's fleets must be reopened for Chinese commerce.

conditions.text: Chose Maritime Ascendancy
Own Malacca, or a subject owns it
A market the country is in

children.text: Silk is produced in the market
Silk is traded in the market

conditions.text: Gold at least 1000

event.title: The Sea Routes Reopened
event.text:
The Strait of Malacca, that narrow passage through which half the world's trade must flow, now answers to the Dragon Throne. Chinese merchants, freed from the restrictions of the Haijin, are already establishing trading posts and warehouses in every port from Java to Siam.

The silk that once traveled overland on the backs of camels now moves by sea in the holds of junks, faster and in far greater quantity. The maritime silk road is reborn, and this time it flies the Dragon Banner.

options.text: The treasure fleets sail once more

destiny.name: The Treasure Fleet Ascendant
destiny.text: Zheng He's voyages proved that China could project power across the Indian Ocean. Now make that projection permanent. Secure Palembang and Calicut, the gateways to the Spice Islands and the Malabar Coast, and fill the treasury that keeps the fleet at sea.

conditions.text: Own Palembang, or a subject owns it
Own Kozhikode, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 2000

event.title: The Treasure Fleet Ascendant
event.text:
Chinese naval power now stretches from the Spice Islands to the Malabar Coast. Palembang and Calicut, the twin gateways of the Indian Ocean, operate under imperial authority. The treasure fleet has achieved what Zheng He could only demonstrate: permanent Chinese dominion over the maritime world.

The silver that flows into China from this oceanic empire is staggering. The question is how to channel it. Some advocate reinvesting in the trade network itself: better intelligence, more diplomatic connections, a web of commercial relationships that makes Chinese trade indispensable. Others push for naval supremacy pure and simple: faster ships, better-trained crews, a fleet that can project power anywhere.

options.text: The silver tide enriches the entire realm

modifiers.name: Silver Tide
modifiers.text: The flow of silver through Chinese-controlled trade routes enriches every corner of the realm. Raw materials pour from overseas territories while diplomatic connections multiply.

options.text: Naval dominance secures the trade routes

modifiers.name: Fleet Dominance
modifiers.text: The treasure fleet's light squadrons patrol every sea lane. Fast-moving naval forces project power far from home, though land forces receive less attention.

destiny.name: Dragon Banner Over Every Shore
destiny.text: From Hormuz at the mouth of the Persian Gulf to Mogadishu on the African coast to Temasek at the crossroads of all Asian trade: the Dragon Banner must fly over every major port of the maritime world. Build the Treasure Wharf to sustain this unprecedented naval enterprise.

conditions.text: Own Hormuz, or a subject owns it
Own Mogadishu, or a subject owns it
Own Temasek, or a subject owns it
Prestige at least 75
Gold at least 3000

event.title: Dragon Banner Over Every Shore
event.text:
From the Persian Gulf to the coast of Africa, from the straits of Southeast Asia to the harbors of India: every major port of the maritime world now acknowledges Chinese supremacy. The treasure fleet dwarfs any rival navy. Chinese merchants dominate every market they enter.

This is an achievement without historical parallel. The question now is whether to use this maritime supremacy for military purposes (projecting the empire's power into every theater, reducing the cost of overseas warfare) or for economic ones, using the maritime silk road as a highway of trade that enriches the realm through commerce and mercenary recruitment rather than conquest.

options.text: The ocean itself is the empire's domain

modifiers.name: Ocean Sovereign
modifiers.text: The empire projects military power across every ocean. Overseas campaigns are launched with ease, and supply lines stretch to the ends of the earth.

options.text: Let the maritime silk road bind the world

modifiers.name: Silk Road of the Sea
modifiers.text: The maritime silk road generates such wealth that the empire can afford mercenary armies and reduced military costs. The only danger is the complacency that wealth engenders.

units.name: Shenjiying
units.text: The Divine Machine Battalion: elite gunpowder infantry armed with hand cannons, matchlocks, and rocket launchers. Founded as one of three elite capital garrison divisions, the Shenjiying represents China's mastery of the firearms revolution it invented.

units.name: Shenjiying Levy
units.text: Provincial garrison troops trained in the Shenjiying tradition of gunpowder warfare.

units.name: War Junk
units.text: A heavily-armed ocean-going junk built for naval combat. Featuring watertight compartments, large crew quarters, and heavy armament, the war junk is the backbone of Chinese naval power.

units.name: Fuchuan
units.text: The 'blessed ship': a large, flat-bottomed warship armed with bronze cannons and fire arrows. The fuchuan can navigate both coastal shallows and open ocean, carrying larger crews and heavier armament than standard warships.

units.name: War Junk Levy
units.text: A levy-raised war junk crewed by coastal populations with generations of seafaring tradition.

buildings.name: Imperial Examination Hall
buildings.text: A state-administered compound where candidates sit the imperial examinations, competing for positions in the civil service through mastery of the Confucian classics, literary composition, and policy analysis.

buildings.name: Imperial Porcelain Kiln
buildings.text: A state-supervised kiln complex producing porcelain of the highest quality for imperial use and export. The division of labor (with separate specialists for shaping, glazing, painting, and firing) enables production at industrial scale.

buildings.name: Coastal Defense Fort
buildings.text: A fortified coastal installation combining a watchtower, garrison barracks, and naval patrol station. Part of the empire's chain of maritime defenses against piracy and foreign intrusion.

buildings.name: Grand Shipyard
buildings.text: A massive shipbuilding facility capable of constructing the largest vessels in the world. Multiple dry docks, timber yards, and outfitting berths allow simultaneous construction of war junks and treasure ships.

buildings.name: Nanjing Arsenal
buildings.text: A modern armaments factory producing firearms, artillery, and ammunition using Western industrial methods. The arsenal represents the Self-Strengthening Movement's commitment to military modernization.

buildings.name: Forbidden Palace
buildings.text: The supreme administrative complex of the universal empire: a vast palace compound from which the Son of Heaven governs All Under Heaven. Its halls house the most extensive bureaucracy in human history, its archives contain the records of every province, and its examination chambers produce the scholar-officials who administer an empire without equal.

buildings.name: Treasure Wharf
buildings.text: A massive naval complex purpose-built for the treasure fleet: multiple dry docks, timber stores, sail lofts, and outfitting berths capable of constructing and maintaining the largest warships and merchantmen the world has ever seen. From this wharf, the Dragon Banner is carried to every shore.

list.name: Imperial Examination System
list.text: Codified by the Sui in 605 and brought to maturity under the Tang and Song, the Keju selected officials by competitive written examination on the Confucian classics. Sheng-yuan, Juren, and Jinshi degrees defined a literate scholar-official class loyal to the throne over hereditary aristocrats. The Ming intensified the system in 1370 and the Qing maintained it until its formal abolition in 1905, producing a meritocratic civilian government but permanently barring the great clans from the highest offices and inviting endemic cheating, factionalism, and degree-sale during periods of decline.

list.name: Three Provincial Commissions
list.text: In 1376 the Hongwu Emperor abolished the branch secretariats the Yuan had left behind and divided each province between three offices: one for administration and tax, one for justice and surveillance, one for the garrisons. None could give orders to the others, and each answered to a different office in the capital. No governor could turn a province into a kingdom of his own. The price was three offices that quarrelled over every boundary between them, until the court began sending grand coordinators to make them work together.

list.name: Offices of Scrutiny
list.text: Six small offices, one beside each ministry. Their supervising secretaries read every edict and memorial that passed, kept a copy, and could send an edict back unissued. From 1573 they also held the register of deadlines by which each ministry was judged. They answered to no minister, and they stood outside the Censorate until the Yongzheng Emperor merged the two in 1723. At their best they stopped a bad order before it went out. At their worst they were the trenches of every factional war at court.

list.name: Hanlin Academy
list.text: Founded under the Tang and elevated by the Song, the Hanlin Yuan was the empire's elite literary institute. Drawn from the highest jinshi graduates, its members drafted imperial edicts, compiled the dynastic histories, tutored the heir apparent, and curated orthodoxy. The Academy lent the throne unmatched cultural legitimacy, but a coddled academician class tended to crystallize into factional cliques whose endorsement of the emperor's actions grew increasingly hollow.

list.name: Office of Transmission
list.text: Founded by the Hongwu Emperor in 1377. Every memorial to the throne came through it, whether from a provincial official or from a commoner with a grievance. Its clerks copied each one, entered it in a register, and sent the original up. The emperor heard from every province, and no minister stood between him and the paper. Whoever held the office could also hold a memorial back, and under weak emperors that is what happened.

conditions.text: Owns Dàdū

list.name: Office of the Imperial Eunuchs
list.text: The Si-li Jian, headed by the Director of Ceremonial, emerged in the Yongle era as the eunuch bureau holding the imperial seal. Eunuchs, owing loyalty only to the throne, allowed emperors to bypass the scholar-bureaucracy and run a parallel administration. The system produced ruthlessly efficient autocracies under Zhengde and Wanli. But also the notorious dictatorships of Wang Zhen, Liu Jin, and Wei Zhongxian, which discredited the dynasty and accelerated the Ming collapse.

list.name: Lifan Yuan
list.text: Established by Hong Taiji in 1638 and elevated to ministerial rank by the Qing, the Lifan Yuan, Court of Colonial Affairs, administered Mongolia, Tibet, and later Xinjiang through a separate apparatus from the Six Ministries. Operating in Mongolian, Tibetan, and Manchu as well as Chinese, it managed the leagues and banners, supervised the Dalai Lama's court, and structured tributary relations with Inner Asian polities. Its dual-track frontier governance held the steppe loyal so long as the dynasty remained vigorous; neglect invited Junggar revolt and the long unraveling of the imperial frontier.
